title: Maximum Subarray Sum
description: Given an integer array nums, find the contiguous non-empty subarray with the largest sum and return that sum.
hints: A subarray ending at index i either extends the best subarray ending at i-1 or starts fresh at i.
You only need the best sum ending at the previous index, not the whole table.
solution_explanation: Kadane's algorithm. Keep cur, the best sum of a subarray that ends at the current element: cur = max(x, cur + x). A negative running sum can only hurt the next element, so it is dropped. The answer is the maximum cur seen. One pass, constant memory.
name: maxSubarraySum

title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock
description: prices[i] is the price of a stock on day i. Pick one day to buy and a later day to sell. Return the maximum profit you can make, or 0 if no profit is possible.
hints: For a fixed selling day, the best buying day is the cheapest day before it.
Track the lowest price seen so far while scanning once.
solution_explanation: Scan left to right keeping the lowest price so far. At each day the best profit if you sell today is price - lowest. Take the maximum over all days. Because you only look back at one running minimum, a single pass is enough.
name: maxProfit

title: Product of Array Except Self
description: Return an array answer where answer[i] is the product of every element of nums except nums[i]. Do not use division.
constraints:
2 <= nums.length <= 10^4
-30 <= nums[i] <= 30
Every prefix and suffix product fits in a 32-bit integer.
hints: answer[i] = (product of everything left of i) x (product of everything right of i).
Build the left products in one pass and multiply the right products in a second pass.
solution_explanation: Fill answer with prefix products (answer[i] holds the product of nums[0..i-1]). Then walk from the right with a running suffix product and multiply it into answer[i]. No division, so zeros need no special case.
name: productExceptSelf

title: Rotate Array Right
description: Return a new array that is nums rotated to the right by k steps. Rotating by one step moves the last element to the front.
hints: Rotating by the array length changes nothing, so reduce k first.
The last k elements move to the front, in order.
solution_explanation: Reduce k modulo the length. The answer is the last k elements followed by the first n-k. The in-place variant reverses the whole array, then reverses the first k and the last n-k elements.
name: rotateRight

title: Move Zeroes to the End
description: Return the array with all zeros moved to the end while the non-zero elements keep their original relative order.
hints: Keep a write pointer for the next non-zero slot.
After copying the non-zeros forward, fill the rest with zeros.
solution_explanation: Walk the array once; every non-zero value is written at the write pointer, which then advances. Everything from the pointer to the end becomes zero. Order of non-zeros is preserved because we never reorder them.
name: moveZeroes

title: Missing Number
description: nums holds n distinct numbers taken from the range 0 to n. Return the one number in that range that is missing.
hints: The sum of 0..n is known.
Compare it with the sum of the array.
solution_explanation: The numbers 0..n sum to n(n+1)/2. Subtract the actual sum of the array; what is left is the missing value. An XOR of all indices and values works too and cannot overflow.
name: missingNumber

title: Single Number
description: Every element of nums appears exactly twice except one, which appears once. Return that single element.
constraints:
1 <= nums.length <= 3 x 10^4 and nums.length is odd
-3 x 10^4 <= nums[i] <= 3 x 10^4
hints: What happens when you XOR a number with itself?
XOR is order-independent.
solution_explanation: x ^ x = 0 and x ^ 0 = x. XOR-ing the whole array cancels every pair and leaves the single value, in one pass and no extra memory.
name: singleNumber

title: Majority Element
description: Return the element that appears more than n/2 times in nums, where n is the length. A majority element always exists.
constraints:
1 <= nums.length <= 5 x 10^4
-10^9 <= nums[i] <= 10^9
A majority element is guaranteed.
hints: Could you cancel pairs of different elements?
A true majority survives all the cancellations.
solution_explanation: Boyer-Moore voting: keep a candidate and a count. Equal element increments, a different one decrements, and at zero the next element becomes the candidate. A value occupying more than half the slots cannot be cancelled out, so it is the last candidate standing.
name: majorityElement

title: Merge Two Sorted Arrays
description: Given two arrays sorted in non-decreasing order, return one sorted array containing all their elements.
hints: Compare the front elements of both arrays and take the smaller one.
When one array runs out, append the rest of the other.
solution_explanation: Two pointers, one per array. Repeatedly take the smaller front element. Each element is moved once, so the merge is linear — the same step merge sort relies on.
name: mergeSorted

title: Find All Duplicates
description: Return, in ascending order, every value that appears two or more times in nums. Each duplicated value is listed once.
hints: A hash set remembers what you have already seen.
Collect repeats in another set so each is reported once, then sort.
solution_explanation: Walk the array with a "seen" set; a value met a second time goes into a "duplicates" set. Sorting the duplicates at the end gives the required order.
name: findDuplicates

title: Subarray Sum Equals K
description: Count the contiguous subarrays of nums whose elements add up to exactly k.
hints: The sum of nums[i..j] equals prefix[j+1] - prefix[i].
For each prefix, how many earlier prefixes equal prefix - k?
solution_explanation: Keep a running prefix sum and a map from prefix value to how many times it occurred. A subarray ending here sums to k exactly when an earlier prefix equals (current - k), so add that count. Negative numbers are fine because we never shrink a window.
name: subarraySum

title: Sort Colors
description: nums contains only 0, 1 and 2 (think of three colours). Return it sorted in ascending order without calling a library sort.
hints: Counting the three values and rewriting works in two passes.
Can you do it in one pass with three regions: 0s, 1s and unknown, 2s?
solution_explanation: Dutch national flag. Keep pointers lo, mid, hi. Swap 0s behind lo, leave 1s, swap 2s past hi. The region between mid and hi is the unsorted part and shrinks every step.
name: sortColors

title: Jump Game
description: You start at index 0. nums[i] is the maximum number of steps you can jump forward from index i. Return true if you can reach the last index.
hints: What is the furthest index you can reach so far?
If you are standing past the furthest reachable index, you are stuck.
solution_explanation: Greedy reach. Walk the array tracking the furthest reachable index. If the current index exceeds it, the path is blocked; otherwise extend the reach with i + nums[i]. If the scan finishes, the end is reachable.
name: jump

title: Valid Palindrome
description: A phrase is a palindrome if, after removing every character that is not a letter or digit and ignoring upper/lower case, it reads the same forwards and backwards. Return true if s is a palindrome.
constraints:
0 <= s.length <= 2 x 10^5
s contains printable ASCII characters.
hints: Two pointers moving inward, skipping characters that do not count.
Compare lower-cased characters.
solution_explanation: Keep one pointer at each end. Skip anything that is not alphanumeric, compare the lower-cased characters, and move inward. A mismatch means not a palindrome; meeting in the middle means it is.
name: isPalindrome

tests.input: s = "A man, a plan, a canal: Panama"

title: Longest Common Prefix
description: Return the longest string that is a prefix of every string in strs, or an empty string if there is none.
constraints:
1 <= strs.length <= 200
0 <= strs[i].length <= 200
Lowercase English letters only.
hints: Start with the first word as the candidate prefix.
Shorten the candidate until each other word starts with it.
solution_explanation: Take the first string as the prefix and, for every other string, chop characters off the end of the prefix until the string starts with it. The remaining prefix is common to all.
name: longestCommonPrefix

title: Reverse Words in a String
description: Words are separated by one or more spaces. Return a string with the words in reverse order, joined by a single space, with no leading or trailing spaces.
constraints:
1 <= s.length <= 10^4
s has at least one word.
hints: Splitting on whitespace removes the extra spaces for you.
Reverse the list of words and join.
solution_explanation: Split on runs of whitespace, reverse the list, join with one space. Splitting that way drops leading, trailing and repeated spaces automatically.
name: reverseWords
reference_python:
def reverseWords(s):
    return ' '.join(s.split()[::-1])

title: Is Subsequence
description: s is a subsequence of t if you can delete some (possibly none) characters from t, without reordering the rest, and get s. Return true if it is.
hints: Walk through t once.
Advance a pointer in s only when the characters match.
solution_explanation: Greedy matching: scan t, and every time t[j] equals s[i] move i forward. If i reaches the end of s, every character was matched in order.
name: isSubsequence

title: Isomorphic Strings
description: Two strings are isomorphic if the characters of s can be replaced to get t, with every occurrence of a character replaced by the same one and no two different characters mapping to the same one. Return true if they are isomorphic.
hints: You need the mapping to work in both directions.
Two dictionaries, or compare "first occurrence" patterns.
solution_explanation: Maintain a map s->t and a map t->s. If a character is already mapped to something different in either direction the strings are not isomorphic. Both maps are needed: "ab" and "aa" must be rejected.
name: isIsomorphic

title: First Unique Character
description: Return the index of the first character in s that appears exactly once, or -1 if there is none.
hints: Count every character first.
Then scan again for the first one whose count is 1.
solution_explanation: Two passes: build a frequency table, then walk the string again and return the first index whose count is 1. The second pass keeps the original order.
name: firstUniqueChar

title: Ransom Note
description: Return true if note can be built from the letters of magazine, using each magazine letter at most once.
hints: Count the letters available.
Every letter of the note must be available at least as many times as needed.
solution_explanation: Count letters in the magazine and in the note. The note can be built exactly when, for each letter, the magazine count is at least the note count.
name: canConstruct

title: Longest Palindromic Substring (Length)
description: Return the length of the longest substring of s that is a palindrome.
hints: Every palindrome has a centre — a character or a gap between two.
Expand outward from each centre while both ends match.
solution_explanation: Try all 2n-1 centres and expand while the characters on both sides are equal; track the longest span. It is quadratic but simple and fast enough for n up to 1000. (Manacher's algorithm makes it linear.)
name: longestPalindromeLength

title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
description: Return the length of the longest substring of s in which no character appears twice.
hints: Keep a window [start, i] with all distinct characters.
When a repeat appears, jump start just past its previous position.
solution_explanation: Sliding window with a map of the last index of each character. When s[i] was last seen inside the current window, move the window start to one past that index. The window length at each step is a candidate answer.
name: lengthOfLongestSubstring

title: String Compression
description: Compress s by replacing each run of the same character with the character followed by the run length. A run of length 1 stays as just the character. Return the compressed string.
hints: Walk the string tracking the length of the current run.
Write the count only when it is greater than 1.
solution_explanation: Scan once, counting how long the current character repeats. When the run ends, append the character and, if the run is longer than one, its length.
name: compressString

title: Valid Brackets
description: s contains only the characters ( ) [ ] { }. Return true if every opening bracket is closed by the same type of bracket, in the correct order.
hints: The most recent unclosed bracket must be closed first.
That is last-in, first-out.
solution_explanation: Push opening brackets on a stack. A closing bracket must match the top of the stack, which is popped. The string is valid if no mismatch happens and the stack is empty at the end.
name: validParentheses

title: Climbing Stairs
description: You climb a staircase of n steps, taking 1 or 2 steps at a time. In how many distinct ways can you reach the top?
hints: To stand on step n you came from step n-1 or n-2.
ways(n) = ways(n-1) + ways(n-2).
solution_explanation: The last move was either 1 or 2 steps, so ways(n) = ways(n-1) + ways(n-2) — the Fibonacci recurrence. Keep only the last two values for constant memory.
name: climbStairs

title: House Robber
description: nums[i] is the money in house i along a street. You cannot rob two adjacent houses. Return the most money you can rob.
hints: At each house you either rob it (and skipped the previous one) or skip it.
Track the best total if the previous house was robbed and if it was skipped.
solution_explanation: Two running values: take (best total with the current house robbed) and skip (best total without it). Robbing needs the previous "skip"; skipping takes the larger of the previous two. The answer is the larger at the end.
name: rob

title: Coin Change
description: You have unlimited coins of each denomination in coins. Return the fewest coins needed to make exactly amount, or -1 if it cannot be made.
hints: Define dp[a] = fewest coins for amount a.
dp[a] = 1 + min(dp[a - c]) over coins c <= a.
solution_explanation: Bottom-up table of the fewest coins for every amount from 0 to amount. Each amount tries every coin as the last one. Amounts that stay at infinity are unreachable.
name: coinChange

title: Longest Increasing Subsequence
description: Return the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence of nums (elements need not be adjacent).
hints: A simple dp[i] = longest ending at i is O(n^2).
Keep, for each length, the smallest possible tail value — it stays sorted, so binary search it.
solution_explanation: Patience-sorting idea: tails[k] is the smallest tail of an increasing subsequence of length k+1. For each number, find the first tail >= it by binary search and replace it (or append if none). The final length of tails is the answer.
name: lengthOfLIS

title: Unique Paths
description: A robot starts at the top-left of an m x n grid and can only move right or down. How many different paths lead to the bottom-right corner?
constraints:
1 <= m, n <= 100
The answer fits in a 64-bit integer.
hints: Paths to a cell = paths from above + paths from the left.
The first row and column each have exactly one path.
solution_explanation: dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j] + dp[i][j-1]. One row of memory is enough: update it in place left to right. (It equals the binomial coefficient C(m+n-2, m-1).)
name: uniquePaths

title: Edit Distance
description: Return the minimum number of operations to turn string a into string b. An operation inserts a character, deletes a character, or replaces a character.
hints: dp[i][j] is the distance between the first i letters of a and the first j letters of b.
If the last letters match, copy dp[i-1][j-1]; otherwise take 1 + the smallest of insert, delete, replace.
solution_explanation: Classic table. When a[i-1] == b[j-1] the cost is dp[i-1][j-1]; otherwise 1 + min(dp[i-1][j] (delete), dp[i][j-1] (insert), dp[i-1][j-1] (replace)). Only the previous row is needed.
name: minDistance

title: Longest Common Subsequence
description: Return the length of the longest subsequence that appears in both strings (characters in order, not necessarily adjacent), or 0 if there is none.
hints: dp[i][j] = LCS of the first i letters of a and first j of b.
Matching last letters extend the LCS by one; otherwise take the better of dropping a letter from either string.
solution_explanation: If a[i-1] == b[j-1] then dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1, else max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]). The bottom-right cell is the answer; two rolling rows keep memory small.
name: longestCommonSubsequence

title: Partition Equal Subset Sum
description: Return true if the positive integers in nums can be split into two groups with equal sums.
hints: If the total is odd the answer is no.
Otherwise can some subset reach total/2? That is a subset-sum question.
solution_explanation: Subset-sum DP: keep the set of reachable sums (here as a bitmask). Adding a number x ORs the set shifted by x into itself. The answer is whether total/2 is reachable.
name: canPartition

title: Word Break
description: Return true if s can be split into a sequence of one or more words from the dictionary words (words may be reused).
hints: dp[i] means the first i letters can be segmented.
dp[i] is true if some j < i has dp[j] true and s[j:i] is a word.
solution_explanation: Prefix table: dp[0] is true; dp[i] is true when there is a split point j with dp[j] true and s[j:i] in the dictionary. A hash set makes the lookup constant time.
name: wordBreak

title: Minimum Path Sum
description: Each cell of a grid holds a non-negative number. Moving only right or down from the top-left to the bottom-right, return the smallest possible sum along a path.
hints: Each cell can only be entered from above or from the left.
cost(cell) = value + min(cost(above), cost(left)).
solution_explanation: Fill a table of the cheapest cost to reach each cell. The first row and column have only one way in. The bottom-right value is the answer.
name: minPathSum

title: Decode Ways
description: A message of digits is decoded using A=1, B=2, ..., Z=26. Return how many different ways the digit string s can be decoded (0 if it cannot be decoded at all).
constraints:
1 <= s.length <= 100
s contains only digits and may start with 0.
hints: A single digit 1-9 is a letter; a leading 0 alone is not.
Two digits form a letter if the pair is between 10 and 26.
solution_explanation: ways(i) = (ways(i-1) if the last digit is non-zero) + (ways(i-2) if the last two digits are 10..26). Keep two rolling values. A string starting with 0 has no decoding.
name: numDecodings

title: Maximum Product Subarray
description: Return the largest product of any contiguous non-empty subarray of nums.
constraints:
1 <= nums.length <= 2 x 10^4
-10 <= nums[i] <= 10
The product always fits in a 32-bit integer.
hints: A negative number can turn the smallest product into the largest.
Track both the maximum and the minimum product ending at each position.
solution_explanation: Keep hi and lo, the largest and smallest product of a subarray ending here. A new element x gives candidates x, hi*x and lo*x (a negative flips them). The answer is the biggest hi seen.
name: maxProductSubarray

title: 0/1 Knapsack
description: Item i has weight weights[i] and value values[i]. You can take each item at most once. Return the largest total value whose total weight does not exceed capacity.
hints: dp[c] = best value with capacity c.
Process items one at a time and loop capacity downwards so an item is used once.
solution_explanation: One-dimensional DP: for each item, for c from capacity down to its weight, dp[c] = max(dp[c], dp[c - w] + v). Iterating downward prevents reusing the same item twice.
name: knapsack

title: Merge Intervals
description: Each interval is [start, end]. Merge all overlapping intervals (touching at a shared endpoint counts as overlapping) and return the result sorted by start.
hints: Sort by start so overlapping intervals become neighbours.
Extend the last merged interval while the next one starts inside it.
solution_explanation: Sort by start. Keep an output list; if the next interval starts at or before the end of the last output interval, extend that end, otherwise start a new interval.
name: mergeIntervals

title: Non-overlapping Intervals
description: Return the minimum number of intervals to remove so that the rest do not overlap. Intervals that only touch at an endpoint do not overlap.
hints: Keeping the most intervals is the same as removing the fewest.
Among intervals, always keep the one that finishes earliest.
solution_explanation: Activity-selection greedy: sort by end time and keep an interval whenever it starts at or after the last kept end. Every interval that cannot be kept is a removal.
name: eraseOverlapIntervals

title: Meeting Rooms
description: Each meeting is [start, end). Return the minimum number of rooms needed so that no two overlapping meetings share a room. A meeting may start exactly when another ends.
hints: Think of people entering and leaving rooms over time.
Sort start and end events; count how many are open at once.
solution_explanation: Turn each meeting into a +1 event at its start and a -1 event at its end; sort events (an end sorts before a start at the same time because -1 < 1). The maximum running total is the room count.
name: minMeetingRooms
reference_python:
def minMeetingRooms(intervals):
    ev = sorted([(s, 1) for s, e in intervals] + [(e, -1) for s, e in intervals])
    cur = best = 0
    for _, d in ev:
        cur += d
        best = max(best, cur)
    return best

title: Gas Station
description: There are stations on a circular route. Station i gives gas[i] fuel and the trip to the next station costs cost[i]. Starting with an empty tank, return the index of the station from which you can drive all the way round, or -1 if that is impossible. If a solution exists it is unique.
hints: If total gas is less than total cost the trip is impossible.
If you run dry between stations a and b, no station between them can be the start.
solution_explanation: First check that total gas covers total cost. Then sweep once keeping the tank; whenever it goes negative, restart from the next station. The final candidate start is the answer.
name: canCompleteCircuit

title: Count Primes
description: Return the number of prime numbers strictly less than n.
hints: Testing every number for primality is slow.
Cross out multiples of each prime instead.
solution_explanation: Sieve of Eratosthenes: mark 0 and 1 as not prime; for each prime p up to sqrt(n) mark p*p, p*p+p, ... as composite. The unmarked numbers are the primes.
name: countPrimes

title: Power of Two
description: Return true if the integer n is a power of two (1, 2, 4, 8, ...).
hints: A power of two has exactly one bit set.
n & (n - 1) clears the lowest set bit.
solution_explanation: For positive n, n & (n-1) removes the lowest set bit, so the result is 0 exactly when only one bit was set. Zero and negatives are not powers of two.
name: isPowerOfTwo
reference_python:
def isPowerOfTwo(n):
    return n > 0 and n & (n - 1) == 0

title: Number of 1 Bits
description: Return the number of 1 bits in the binary representation of the non-negative integer n.
hints: Check the lowest bit, then shift.
Or clear the lowest set bit each time with n & (n - 1).
solution_explanation: Each n & (n-1) removes exactly one set bit, so counting the iterations until n becomes zero gives the population count in time proportional to the number of set bits.
name: hammingWeight

title: Happy Number
description: Replace n by the sum of the squares of its digits, and repeat. n is happy if this process reaches 1; otherwise it loops forever in a cycle that does not include 1. Return true if n is happy.
hints: The sequence either hits 1 or repeats a value.
Remember the values you have seen.
solution_explanation: Simulate the process while recording seen values. Reaching 1 means happy; seeing a repeated value means a cycle, so not happy. (Floyd cycle detection gives O(1) memory.)
name: isHappy

title: Pascal's Triangle Row
description: Return row rowIndex (0-indexed) of Pascal's triangle, where each number is the sum of the two numbers above it.
hints: Each row starts and ends with 1.
Build the next row from the previous one.
solution_explanation: Start from [1] and repeatedly build the next row: 1, then sums of adjacent pairs, then 1. After rowIndex iterations the row is ready.
name: pascalRow

title: Greatest Common Divisor
description: Return the greatest common divisor of two non-negative integers a and b (not both zero).
hints: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a mod b).
When b becomes 0, a is the answer.
solution_explanation: Euclid's algorithm: replace (a, b) by (b, a mod b) until b is 0. The remainder shrinks at least as fast as Fibonacci numbers grow, so it takes O(log min(a, b)) steps.
name: gcdOfTwo

title: Counting Bits
description: Return an array ans of length n + 1 where ans[i] is the number of 1 bits in i.
hints: The bits of i are the bits of i shifted right by one, plus the last bit.
solution_explanation: Dynamic programming on bits: i has the same 1-bits as i >> 1 plus one more if i is odd. One pass fills the whole array.
name: countBits
reference_python:
def countBits(n):
    return [bin(i).count('1') for i in range(n + 1)]

title: Factorial Trailing Zeroes
description: Return the number of trailing zeroes in n! (n factorial).
hints: Each trailing zero comes from a factor 10 = 2 x 5.
There are always more 2s than 5s, so count the 5s.
solution_explanation: Count factors of 5 in 1..n: n/5 + n/25 + n/125 + ... Multiples of 25 contribute an extra 5, and so on. Never compute the factorial itself.
name: trailingZeroes

title: Rotate Image
description: Return an n x n matrix rotated 90 degrees clockwise.
hints: The first row becomes the last column.
Transpose, then reverse every row — or equivalently, reverse the rows then transpose.
solution_explanation: A 90-degree clockwise rotation equals reversing the order of the rows and then transposing. The in-place variant transposes then reverses each row.
name: rotateImage
reference_python:
def rotateImage(matrix):
    return [list(r) for r in zip(*matrix[::-1])]

title: Spiral Matrix
description: Return all elements of an m x n matrix in clockwise spiral order, starting from the top-left.
hints: Take the top row, then turn the remaining matrix.
Peel layers: top, right, bottom, left — shrinking the bounds each time.
solution_explanation: Repeatedly remove the top row and append it, then rotate the remaining rows counter-clockwise so the next edge becomes the top row. Each element is handled once.
name: spiralOrder
reference_python:
def spiralOrder(matrix):
    out = []
    m = [r[:] for r in matrix]
    while m:
        out += m.pop(0)
        m = [list(r) for r in zip(*m)][::-1]
    return out

title: Set Matrix Zeroes
description: If an element of the matrix is 0, set its entire row and column to 0. Return the resulting matrix.
hints: Do not zero things while scanning, or you will create new zeros.
First record which rows and columns contain a zero.
solution_explanation: Two passes: collect the rows and columns that hold a zero, then zero every cell whose row or column was collected. (The O(1)-space version stores the flags in the first row and column.)
name: setZeroes

title: Search a Sorted Matrix
description: Each row of the matrix is sorted ascending, and the first number of each row is greater than the last number of the previous row. Return true if target is in the matrix. Aim for O(log(m x n)).
hints: Read the matrix as one long sorted list.
Index k maps to row k // n and column k % n.
solution_explanation: Treat the matrix as a flat sorted array of m x n values and binary search it, converting the middle index to (row, column) with division and modulo.
name: searchMatrix

title: Number of Islands
description: A grid contains 1 (land) and 0 (water). An island is a group of land cells connected horizontally or vertically. Return the number of islands.
hints: When you find unvisited land, a whole island is discovered.
Flood-fill it (DFS or BFS) so you do not count it again.
solution_explanation: Scan every cell. At an unvisited land cell, increment the island count and flood-fill all connected land with an explicit stack, marking cells visited. Each cell is visited once.
name: numIslands

title: Course Schedule
description: There are numCourses courses labelled 0..numCourses-1. Each pair [a, b] means you must take course b before course a. Return true if you can finish all courses.
constraints:
1 <= numCourses <= 2000
0 <= prerequisites.length <= 5000
All pairs are distinct.
hints: This is asking whether the prerequisite graph has a cycle.
Repeatedly take courses that have no remaining prerequisites.
solution_explanation: Kahn's topological sort: compute in-degrees, queue the courses with none, and repeatedly remove one, lowering its dependents' in-degrees. If all courses get removed there is no cycle.
name: canFinish
reference_python:
def canFinish(numCourses, prerequisites):
    from collections import deque
    adj = [[] for _ in range(numCourses)]
    indeg = [0] * numCourses
    for a, b in prerequisites:
        adj[b].append(a)
        indeg[a] += 1
    q = deque(i for i in range(numCourses) if indeg[i] == 0)
    done = 0
    while q:
        u = q.popleft()
        done += 1
        for v in adj[u]:
            indeg[v] -= 1
            if indeg[v] == 0:
                q.append(v)
    return done == numCourses

title: Rotting Oranges
description: In a grid, 0 is empty, 1 is a fresh orange and 2 is a rotten orange. Every minute, each fresh orange next to (up, down, left, right) a rotten one becomes rotten. Return the minutes until no fresh orange remains, or -1 if that never happens.
hints: All rotten oranges spread at the same time — think of a multi-source BFS.
Process the queue one minute (one level) at a time.
solution_explanation: Multi-source BFS: start with every rotten orange in the queue and expand level by level, each level being one minute. If fresh oranges remain when the queue empties, the answer is -1.
name: orangesRotting
reference_python:
def orangesRotting(grid):
    from collections import deque
    R, C = len(grid), len(grid[0])
    g = [r[:] for r in grid]
    q = deque((i, j) for i in range(R) for j in range(C) if g[i][j] == 2)
    fresh = sum(v == 1 for r in g for v in r)
    t = 0
    while q and fresh:
        for _ in range(len(q)):
            x, y = q.popleft()
            for dx, dy in ((1, 0), (-1, 0), (0, 1), (0, -1)):
                a, b = x + dx, y + dy
                if 0 <= a < R and 0 <= b < C and g[a][b] == 1:
                    g[a][b] = 2
                    fresh -= 1
                    q.append((a, b))
        t += 1
    return t if fresh == 0 else -1

title: Shortest Path in a Binary Matrix
description: In an n x n grid of 0s (open) and 1s (blocked), find the length of the shortest path from the top-left to the bottom-right moving through open cells in any of 8 directions. The length counts the cells visited. Return -1 if no path exists.
constraints:
n == grid.length == grid[i].length
1 <= n <= 100
grid[i][j] is 0 or 1
hints: Every move costs the same, so a plain BFS finds the shortest path.
Remember to check that the start and end cells are open.
solution_explanation: Breadth-first search from the start, expanding in 8 directions and recording the distance. The first time the target is dequeued the distance is minimal because BFS explores by increasing path length.
name: shortestPathBinaryMatrix

title: Subsets
description: Given an array of distinct integers, return every possible subset (the power set), including the empty subset. The order of subsets and of elements inside them does not matter.
constraints:
0 <= nums.length <= 10
-10 <= nums[i] <= 10
All values are distinct.
hints: Each element is either in a subset or not: 2^n choices.
Start from [[]] and, for each number, add a copy of every existing subset with that number included.
solution_explanation: Iterative doubling: begin with the empty subset; for each number x, append x to a copy of every subset built so far. After n numbers there are 2^n subsets.
name: subsets

title: Permutations
description: Return all possible orderings of an array of distinct integers, in any order.
hints: Choose the first element, then permute the rest.
Track which elements are already used.
solution_explanation: Backtracking: at each position try every unused number, recurse, then undo the choice. There are n! complete permutations.
name: permute

title: Combination Sum
description: Given distinct positive integers candidates and a target, return all unique combinations of candidates that sum to target. A number may be used any number of times. Order does not matter.
hints: Decide for each candidate: use it again, or move on.
Stop when the remaining total hits 0 (record) or goes negative (abandon).
solution_explanation: Backtracking over candidate positions. At position i, either take candidates[i] (staying at i so it can repeat) or skip to i+1. A path with remaining 0 is a solution, and moving forward only avoids duplicate orderings.
name: combinationSum

title: Container With Most Water
description: height[i] is the height of a vertical line at position i. Choose two lines that, together with the x-axis, form a container holding the most water. Return that maximum area. The container cannot be slanted.
hints: The area between lines i and j is min(height[i], height[j]) x (j - i).
Start with the widest container. Which line should you move to have any chance of a larger area?
solution_explanation: Two pointers from both ends. Area is limited by the shorter line, so moving the taller line inward can only reduce width without raising the limit. Always move the shorter side; every skipped pair is provably no better.
name: maxArea

title: 3Sum
description: Return all unique triplets [a, b, c] from nums such that a + b + c = 0. The answer must not contain duplicate triplets; the order of triplets and of numbers inside a triplet does not matter.
hints: Sorting makes duplicates adjacent and enables two pointers.
Fix the first number, then solve a sorted two-sum for the rest. Skip repeated first numbers.
solution_explanation: Sort. For each index i (skipping repeated values) run two pointers l and r over the rest: a sum below zero moves l up, above zero moves r down, and a hit records the triplet and skips repeated l values. Sorting costs O(n log n); the pointer sweeps cost O(n^2).
name: threeSum

title: Two Sum in a Sorted Array
description: numbers is sorted in non-decreasing order. Return the 1-based positions [i, j], i < j, of the two numbers that add up to target. Exactly one solution exists.
constraints:
2 <= numbers.length <= 3 x 10^4
-1000 <= numbers[i] <= 1000
Exactly one solution exists.
hints: A sorted array lets you decide which end to move.
If the sum is too small move the left pointer right; too big, move the right pointer left.
solution_explanation: Pointers at both ends. The sum of the two ends is compared with the target: smaller means the left value must grow, larger means the right value must shrink. They converge on the unique pair.
name: twoSumSorted

title: Squares of a Sorted Array
description: nums is sorted in non-decreasing order and may contain negatives. Return the squares of each number, also sorted in non-decreasing order.
hints: The largest square is at one of the two ends.
Fill the answer from the back.
solution_explanation: The biggest absolute value is always at the left or right end. Compare the two ends, place the larger square at the back of the output, and move that pointer inward. This avoids a full sort.
name: sortedSquares

title: Maximum Sum of a Window
description: Return the largest sum of any k consecutive elements of nums.
hints: Recomputing each window from scratch repeats work.
Moving the window by one adds one element and removes one.
solution_explanation: Compute the first window's sum, then slide: add the entering element, subtract the leaving one, and keep the maximum. Each element enters and leaves once.
name: maxSumWindow
reference_python:
def maxSumWindow(nums, k):
    s = sum(nums[:k])
    best = s
    for i in range(k, len(nums)):
        s += nums[i] - nums[i - k]
        best = max(best, s)
    return best

title: Minimum Size Subarray Sum
description: All numbers in nums are positive. Return the length of the shortest contiguous subarray whose sum is at least target, or 0 if no such subarray exists.
hints: Because all numbers are positive, adding elements only increases the sum.
Grow the window on the right; shrink it from the left while the sum still meets the target.
solution_explanation: Expand the right edge, adding to the running sum. While the sum is at least target, record the window length and shrink from the left. Positivity guarantees that shrinking never needs to be undone, so each index is visited at most twice.
name: minSubArrayLen

title: Longest Repeating Character Replacement
description: You may change at most k characters of s to any uppercase letter. Return the length of the longest substring that can be made of one repeated letter.
constraints:
1 <= s.length <= 10^5
0 <= k <= s.length
Uppercase English letters.
hints: A window is valid if (length - count of its most common letter) <= k.
You never need to shrink the recorded best, so the maximum count only needs to grow.
solution_explanation: Sliding window with letter counts. The cost to unify a window is its length minus the count of its most frequent letter. If that cost exceeds k, move the left edge. The maximum valid window length seen is the answer.
name: characterReplacement

title: Permutation in String
description: Return true if s2 contains a substring that is a permutation of s1 (the same letters, any order).
hints: Any permutation of s1 has the same letter counts as s1.
Slide a window of length |s1| across s2 and compare counts.
solution_explanation: Count the letters of s1. Slide a window of the same length over s2, updating the counts incrementally (add the new letter, drop the old one) and compare to s1's counts after every move.
name: checkInclusion

title: Sliding Window Maximum
description: A window of size k slides from the left of nums to the right, one position at a time. Return the maximum value inside the window at each position.
hints: Checking every window costs O(n k).
Keep a queue of indices whose values are in decreasing order — smaller values behind a bigger one can never be the maximum.
solution_explanation: Monotonic deque of indices. Before pushing index i, pop smaller values from the back (they can never beat nums[i] while it is in the window). Pop the front if it has left the window. The front is always the current maximum. Each index is pushed and popped once.
name: maxSlidingWindow

title: Daily Temperatures
description: For each day, return how many days you must wait for a warmer temperature. If no warmer day follows, use 0.
hints: Brute force compares each day with all later days.
Keep a stack of days that are still waiting for a warmer one.
solution_explanation: Monotonic stack of indices with decreasing temperatures. When today is warmer than the day on top, that day has found its answer (the index difference). Pop and repeat, then push today. Each day is pushed and popped once.
name: dailyTemperatures

title: Evaluate Reverse Polish Notation
description: Evaluate an arithmetic expression in Reverse Polish Notation. Valid operators are + - * and /. Division truncates toward zero. The expression is always valid.
constraints:
1 <= tokens.length <= 10^4
Each token is an operator or an integer in [-200, 200].
No division by zero.
hints: Operands come before their operator.
Push numbers; on an operator pop two, apply, push the result.
solution_explanation: Scan left to right with a stack. A number is pushed. An operator pops the right operand then the left operand, applies itself, and pushes the result. Truncate division toward zero (not floor). The final stack top is the value.
name: evalRPN

title: Next Greater Element
description: For each element, return the first greater element that appears to its right, or -1 if there is none.
hints: Which elements are still "waiting" for a greater value?
A stack holds them, and the waiting values are in non-increasing order.
solution_explanation: Scan left to right with a stack of indices whose answer is unknown. A new value resolves every smaller value on top of the stack. Remaining indices have no greater element and keep -1.
name: nextGreater

title: Largest Rectangle in Histogram
description: heights[i] is the height of a histogram bar of width 1. Return the area of the largest rectangle that fits inside the histogram.
hints: A rectangle is limited by its shortest bar.
For each bar, how far can it extend left and right before meeting a shorter bar?
solution_explanation: Monotonic stack of (start index, height) with increasing heights. When a shorter bar arrives, pop taller bars: each popped bar spans from its start to the current index, giving a candidate area; the new bar inherits the earliest start among the popped ones. A sentinel 0 at the end flushes the stack.
name: largestRectangle

title: Generate Parentheses
description: Return every well-formed string of n pairs of round brackets. The order of the strings does not matter.
hints: You can add "(" while fewer than n have been used.
You can add ")" only if it closes an already open bracket.
solution_explanation: Backtracking. Build the string left to right, tracking opened and closed counts. Add "(" if opened < n, and ")" if closed < opened. Every complete string of length 2n built this way is valid, and none is missed. The count is the Catalan number.
name: generateParenthesis

title: Binary Search
description: nums is sorted in ascending order and has no duplicates. Return the index of target, or -1 if it is not present. Aim for O(log n).
constraints:
1 <= nums.length <= 10^4
All values are distinct and sorted ascending.
hints: Look at the middle element first.
Each comparison lets you discard half of the remaining range.
solution_explanation: Keep a range [l, r]. Compare the middle value with target: equal returns the index, smaller moves l past the middle, bigger moves r before it. The range halves each step.
name: search

title: Search Insert Position
description: nums is sorted and has distinct values. Return the index of target if it is present; otherwise return the index where it would be inserted to keep the array sorted.
hints: This is "the first index whose value is >= target".
A lower-bound binary search finds it.
solution_explanation: Lower-bound search on a half-open range [l, r): if nums[m] < target the answer is right of m, otherwise m could be the answer. When l == r it is the first position not less than target.
name: searchInsert

title: Search in Rotated Sorted Array
description: A sorted array of distinct values was rotated at an unknown pivot (for example [0,1,2,4,5,6,7] became [4,5,6,7,0,1,2]). Return the index of target or -1. Aim for O(log n).
hints: At least one half of the range around the middle is always sorted.
Check whether the target lies inside the sorted half.
solution_explanation: Binary search where, at each step, one of the two halves [l..m] or [m..r] is sorted. Test if the target falls inside that sorted half to decide which side to keep.
name: searchRotated

title: First and Last Position of a Value
description: nums is sorted ascending and may contain duplicates. Return [first, last], the first and last index where target occurs, or [-1, -1] if it does not occur. Aim for O(log n).
hints: Two binary searches: one for the left edge, one for the right edge.
The left edge is the first index with value >= target.
solution_explanation: Find the lower bound (first index >= target) and the upper bound (first index > target). If the lower bound does not hold target the answer is [-1, -1]; otherwise it is [lower, upper - 1].
name: searchRange

title: Eating Speed
description: There are piles of bananas. Each hour you choose one pile and eat up to k bananas from it (if the pile has fewer, you finish it and waste the rest of the hour). Return the smallest integer k that lets you finish all piles within h hours.
hints: If k works then any larger k works too.
Binary search on k, checking the hours needed with a loop.
solution_explanation: The answer lies in [1, max(piles)]. For a candidate k the hours needed are the sum of ceil(pile / k). That value only decreases as k grows, so binary search for the smallest k whose hours are at most h.
name: minEatingSpeed

title: Integer Square Root
description: Return the integer part of the square root of the non-negative integer x, without using a built-in square root.
hints: You are looking for the largest m with m x m <= x.
That property holds for small m and fails for large m.
solution_explanation: Binary search on m in [0, x] for the largest value with m*m <= x. Use the upper middle in the loop so the range always shrinks.
name: mySqrt

title: Capacity to Ship Packages
description: Packages must be shipped in the given order, one ship load per day. Each day the ship carries consecutive packages without exceeding its capacity. Return the smallest capacity that ships everything within the given number of days.
hints: The capacity is at least the heaviest package and at most the sum of all.
For a candidate capacity, simulate loading to count days — a larger capacity never needs more days.
solution_explanation: Binary search the capacity between max(weights) and sum(weights). A greedy simulation counts the days needed for a capacity (start a new day when the next package would overflow). Move to the smaller half when the capacity works.
name: shipWithinDays

title: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array
description: A sorted array of distinct values was rotated between 1 and n times. Return its minimum element in O(log n).
hints: Compare the middle value with the last value.
If nums[m] > nums[r], the minimum is to the right of m.
solution_explanation: If the middle element is greater than the rightmost one, the rotation point (the minimum) lies right of the middle; otherwise it is at the middle or to its left. Shrink the range until one element remains.
name: findMin
